content.text:
Comment class: feature
Four answers first, then the plan. Nothing filed and no code written yet — the two decisions at the bottom change what gets written.

## 1. The one-read claim — confirmed, and the merge *removes* reads

`listWorkItems` ([`run.mjs:415`](packs/claudinite-tasks/src/schedule/run.mjs#L415)) already queries `state=all` with `since` = 40 days and projects title, **body**, labels, state and timestamps in one paginated call. That is a superset of both of the janitor's listings — including `listDoneWorkItems`, the input to the superseded-park rule. So the merged pass makes **three paginated listings into two**, not one into three.

Per-item calls, after the merge:

- `listComments` on an item in `task:status:running-executor` — **already made today**
- `listComments` on an item in `task:status:running-agent` — new, and the only new per-item read
- `getIssue` per unresolved `body.blockedBy` — already made today
- `getIssue` per `body.endsWhen` — new, one per approval park, which is a handful at most

**One hazard.** `since` filters on *updated* time, so an item nobody has touched in 40 days is not in the scheduler's listing at all — while the janitor's open listing carries no `since` and does see it. A blocked item idle six weeks is invisible to the merged pass unless the open half is listed unbounded. That's why it's two queries: open with no `since`, closed with it.

## 2. The single-pass claim — true, with one condition that is the whole implementation

The dependency graph is acyclic in the direction you guessed. State rules can change what the ask sees (closing a park releases the task's lane; retiring an orphan removes its item; the unclosed-terminal close turns a `task:status:done` item into evidence for the superseded-park rule). The ask changes nothing any state rule looks at: it creates an issue at `task:status:waiting-for-executor` with age zero, which no state rule selects. So state-then-schedule gives you one pass.

The condition: **the ask must read the effects, not the snapshot.** `planSchedulerRun` already does half of this with `closedByThisRun`, but the cadence terms (`last-run-not-failed` and friends) are evaluated against `items` — the pre-mutation listing. Close a failure park in the state block and the ask will still see it standing, so the lane stays held and the occurrence isn't filed until the next tick. Threading the state block's effects into the item list handed to the ask is what makes the pass genuinely single, and it's the part that needs a test of its own.

Two things that stay: the ordering inside the state block (close terminals before reading done-evidence, or accept a tick of lag on superseded parks), and the per-item `recheck` before writing in the three rules whose premise is a transient. A recheck is a write-time confirm, not a second pass.

## 3. Comments — one dies, and it's a bug

Going through all thirteen write sites: the episode boundary is machine-read protocol, the adopt reply is a person's receipt for their own action, five are park escalations explaining why a human is needed, and six are terminal closes. By your rule, all twelve stay.

The thirteenth is the stuck-dependency comment, and it's worse than noise. [`stuckBlockedItems`](packs/claudinite-tasks/src/recover/janitor-rules.mjs#L113) measures from **`created_at`**, and the sweep has no once-only guard — so once an item is two days old and still blocked, it gets nagged on *every single pass*, forever. Daily today; twice daily after the merge. It changes no state and it is the one rule whose entire output is a comment. It goes.

The real noise is elsewhere, and it's question 4: a heartbeat is one comment per 15 minutes per running item, which dwarfs the whole table.

## 4. The heartbeat — no, nothing touches the Action

Reclaim writes two labels and a comment and returns. There is no cancel call anywhere in the engine; the only Actions writes are cost folding and PR check reads. So a reclaim of a *live but silent* executor leaves two workers on one item — claim arbitration protects the issue, but the orphaned job keeps running its work step and can still push a branch or open a PR.

The arithmetic today: job cap 350 minutes, leash 60 minutes, beat every 15. The beat exists solely so the 60-minute leash doesn't fire on healthy long work — its own header says the run cap retired when the beat landed. So your instinct is right: a TTL below the leash makes silence *imply* death and the beat buys nothing. The cost is that it caps legitimate work at the leash, which is exactly what the beat was introduced to remove.

I'd rather fix the actual hole: **cancel the run at reclaim**. The claim comment already carries the run URL, and both workflows already hold `actions: write`. That makes reclaim correct under either scheme, and then the beat interval is a free dial.

## The plan

Four PRs, written as a stack before any of them is reviewed.

| | Step | Leaves behind | Predicted diff | Policy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Correct the stale cadence prose — ~12 comments claiming an hourly scheduler and ~2h recovery, false since the cron went to two ticks a day | the docs describe the machine that exists | `packs/claudinite-tasks/**` comments + README, no code | `doc-changes` — automerges |
| **B** | The single pass: the queue rules run inside `planSchedulerRun` before the ask; effects threaded into the ask's inputs; open listed unbounded; stuck-dependency rule deleted; dead `supersede` op deleted; sim's `janitorBody` folded into `schedulerBody`; PRINCIPLES.md's three-responsibility split rewritten | one pass, rules still pure in `recover/` | `src/schedule/`, `src/recover/`, `src/items/`, `test/`, `docs/PRINCIPLES.md` | **`nothing`** — every member runs this; a regression disables recovery fleet-wide |
| **C** | Delete the `task-janitor` task whole — declaration, worker, queue-sweep shell, README, its tests | one fewer moving part; `recover/janitor-rules.mjs` survives as the pure module | `tasks/task-janitor/` deleted, `test/tasks/` deleted | **`nothing`** — a deletion |
| **D** | Cancel the executor's Actions run at reclaim, from the claim comment's run URL; re-set the leash/beat arithmetic on the back of it | reclaim can't leave two workers on one item | `src/schedule/run.mjs`, `src/items/heartbeat.mjs`, `test/` | **`nothing`** — it kills a live production job |

**Graph.** A is independent and lands first. B → C → D is serial, because each touches files the previous one rewrote. Then two chain links that can only be read in production: **E** forces a scheduler run and reads its log for one-pass recovery with no janitor item filed (blocked by C); **F** verifies a real reclaim cancels its run (blocked by D). **G**, the retrospective, blocked by F.

**Your workload: 3 human gates** — B, C and D. A automerges; E, F and G are queued runs that come back on their own.

No new design doc: this pack keeps its mechanism in `PRINCIPLES.md` and module headers, and B rewrites the section that this change falsifies.

Two decisions change what I write, so I'm asking before writing rather than after.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- backfilling-provenance: Filling a pack's empty provenance files from its history - each entry derived from the adding commit, its pull request and the version log before the rule is re-read, every commit that touched the pack weighed whether or not a draft covers it, and the README and manifest trimmed to use in the same change. Use when a pack under packs/ or .claudinite/local/packs/ carries empty provenance files, or when asked to backfill or write a pack's provenance.

- searching-for-a-tool: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- working-with-generated-files: Working with a file a test or tool generates — naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, and resolving its merge conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.

Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written - RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon - brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, the marker that names a rule's provenance file. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
- writing-repo-scanning-checks: How a check that scans the repo picks its file set, strips comments before matching a forbidden token, and proves itself silent against real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. - update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. - simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). - security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

input.prompt:
You are reviewing a migration plan for the repo at /home/user/Claudinite before any code is written. Be adversarial and concrete. Read the actual code; do not take the plan's claims on trust.

## Background

The `claudinite-tasks` pack (packs/claudinite-tasks/) runs a queue of work items as GitHub issues. Three components today:
- THE SCHEDULER RUN — `src/schedule/run.mjs`, `planSchedulerRun` + `schedulerRun`. Runs on cron `44 5,17 * * *` (twice a day) per .github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml. Jobs: reap orphans, ask each declared task and create items, ready blocked items, adopt marked issues, reclaim dead executor claims. Ends with a "drain gate" that starts an executor job if anything is pickable.
- THE EXECUTOR — `src/execute/loop.mjs`. Picks one item, claims it, runs it.
- THE JANITOR — a scheduled TASK (`tasks/task-janitor/`), at most daily, whose code-work is `tasks/task-janitor/worker.mjs` (a legacy sweep over retired "[claudinite-task]" dispatch issues) plus `tasks/task-janitor/queue-sweep.mjs` (the real one, a sweep over the work-item queue). Its rules are pure functions in `src/recover/janitor-rules.mjs` (rules A-I).

## The plan to review

ONE pull request, automerge policy `nothing`, containing all of:
A. Correct ~12 stale code comments and README paragraphs claiming the scheduler runs "hourly" and recovery takes "~2h" (false since the cron went to two ticks a day).
B. Fold the janitor's queue rules into `planSchedulerRun` as a state-change phase that runs BEFORE the task-asking phase, so it is one pass. Thread the state phase's effects into the item list handed to the ask (so e.g. a failure park closed in this pass is seen as closed by cadence terms like `last-run-not-failed`). List open items with NO `since` filter and closed items with it. Delete rule C (the stuck-dependency comment rule) entirely. Delete the dead `supersede` op kind in run.mjs. In the simulator (test/sim/sim.mjs) move the `janitorBody` call into `schedulerBody` so scenarios exercise the merged pass. Rewrite docs/PRINCIPLES.md's three-responsibility split.
C. Delete `tasks/task-janitor/` entirely — task.json, worker.mjs (the legacy slot sweep), queue-sweep.mjs, README, and test/tasks/task-janitor-*.test.mjs. Keep `src/recover/janitor-rules.mjs` as the pure module.
D. At reclaim of a dead executor claim, CANCEL the executor's GitHub Actions run (the run URL is in the claim comment; both workflows already have `actions: write`). Re-set the heartbeat/leash arithmetic on the back of that (today: job `timeout-minutes: 350`, `EXECUTING_LEASH_MS` 60m, `HEARTBEAT_MS` 15m).
Then, in the same session after merge: E. force a scheduler run via workflow_dispatch and read its log for one-pass behaviour with no janitor item filed. F. verify a real reclaim cancels its run. G. a production retrospective, deferred as a queued issue.

## Claims the plan rests on — verify each against the code, say TRUE/FALSE/PARTLY and why

1. The merged pass needs no new bulk reads: `listWorkItems` in run.mjs already returns title, body, labels, state and timestamps for open AND closed items, and is a superset of the janitor's `listOpenWorkItems` and `listDoneWorkItems` in src/items/read.mjs.
2. The only new per-item reads are `listComments` on items labelled `task:status:running-agent`, and `getIssue` per `Ends-when:` target.
3. `listWorkItems` uses GitHub's `since` parameter (40 days), which filters on UPDATED time, so an open item untouched for longer is invisible to it — hence the plan's "list open with no since".
4. Ordering state-changes-then-ask makes a single pass sufficient: no rule in the janitor set depends on anything the ask produces, so the dependency graph is acyclic.
5. The cadence/precondition terms are evaluated against the pre-mutation item list, so without threading effects a park closed in the same pass would not release the task's lane until the next tick.
6. `stuckBlockedItems` in src/recover/janitor-rules.mjs measures idleness from `created_at` (not `updated_at`) and the sweep has no once-only guard, so it re-posts its comment on EVERY pass forever once an item is 2 days old and still blocked.
7. The `supersede` op kind in run.mjs is dead: declared and applied but never emitted by the planner.
8. Nothing in the engine cancels a GitHub Actions run; reclaim only writes labels and a comment, so a live-but-silent executor keeps running after its item is reclaimed.
9. The simulator never exercises the janitor as a TASK — it calls `sweepQueue` directly on a daily clock tick, so no test covers the janitor's instantiation, precondition, pickup or converge.

## Also review the plan itself

Read /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-migration-plans/SKILL.md, in particular its "Reviewing someone else's plan" checklist, and apply it. Also read packs/claudinite-tasks/docs/PRINCIPLES.md and .claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md, and flag any repo rule or stated principle this plan violates.

Specifically hunt for:
- Rules in the janitor set that would MISBEHAVE at twice-daily instead of once-daily frequency (re-announcement, repeated comments, clocks that assume a daily cadence, bounds that are multiples of a day).
- Interactions between the janitor rules and the scheduler jobs that the plan has not noticed — especially any rule that could fire on an item the same pass just created or relabelled.
- Anything in `tasks/task-janitor/worker.mjs` (the legacy slot sweep) whose deletion loses behaviour nothing else provides, and who would notice.
- Whether deleting rule C loses a real signal.
- Whether cancelling the Actions run at reclaim can cause harm (e.g. cancelling a run that is doing something else, a run id that is stale, a self-cancel).
- Test coverage that would have to be written for the merged pass, and any existing test that would silently stop asserting anything.

## Output

A tight report: each numbered claim with TRUE/FALSE/PARTLY and the file:line evidence; then a list of findings ranked by what they cost, each with the file:line and a one-line recommendation. No preamble, no summary of what you read. Do not edit any files.
